chunks: And as for what was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar al-Sabati who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman who is among the people of her household, and she dislikes that the people of her household know about her. Is it permissible for her to appoint a man who intends to marry her, saying to him, 'I have appointed you, so bear witness to my marriage'? He said, 'No.' I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, and if she is a virgin (ayyim)?' He said, 'And if she is a virgin.' I said, 'And if she appoints another man for her marriage from him?' He said, 'Yes.'

So this report does not contradict what we have previously mentioned from the reports, because it came in the context of precaution and as the preferable option. Do you not see that the questioner asked and said that she fears that someone will know about her, and the precaution for her was to appoint another man who is not the one marrying her? And if it were not permissible for her to marry herself to the man without a guardian, it would not be permissible for her either to appoint anyone in any case. And that which also indicates what we have mentioned is what was narrated:

key_terms.أَيِّماً: A virgin woman who has not been married before
key_terms.وَلِيٍّ: Guardian (typically the father or male relative in Shia jurisprudence)

ai.seo_question: Can a woman appoint her intended husband as her proxy for marriage to keep it secret from her family?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the permissibility of a woman contracting her own marriage and the specific mechanism of proxy (*wakalah*) when secrecy is desired. The ruling emphasizes *ihtiyat* (precaution) by requiring a third-party proxy rather than the groom himself, ensuring the contract's validity while maintaining privacy, a nuance that complements earlier reports on female agency in marriage. This highlights the Shia juristic view that a woman’s self-contracting is valid but can be optimized through distinct agency to avoid potential complications regarding guardianship or public knowledge.
